links.passage: Application efficiencies of micro- irrigation systems are typically high because these systems distribute wa- ter near or directly into the crop root zone; water losses resulting from wind drift and evaporation are typi- cally small (Boman, 2002; Locascio, 2005).
reference_entries: Boman, B.J. 2002. Efficiency, uniformity, and system evaluation, p. 399–414. In: B.J. Boman (ed.). Water and Florida citrus: Use, regulation, systems, and management. Inst. Food Agr. Sci., Univ. Florida Press, Gainesville, FL.

links.section: Irrigation of vegetables and melons

links.passage: It is thought that drip irrigation gives the higher appli- cation efficiency for vegetables in Florida (80% to 90%) compared with seepage (20% to 50%) and overhead irri- gation systems (60% to 80%) (Simmone et al., 2007).
reference_entries: Simmone, E.H., M.D. Dukes, and D.Z. Haman. 2007. Principles and practices of irrigation management for vegetables. Inst. Food Agr. Sci., Univ. Florida, AE 260.

links.passage: The limited lat- eral water movement in sandy soils under drip irrigation drastically affects the root distribution (Zotarelli et al., 2009) and nutrient interception in the sides of the raised bed (Fig. 6).
supporting_passages: It is also important to point out that preferential pathways lead to dramatic reduction in wetted soil volume and an increase in nutrient leaching, which can be crucial for root development, plant growth, and yield on many vegetables.
links.inference_note: The preceding sentence states that reduced wetted volume and leaching affect root development, growth and yield, and the cited sentence attributes limited lateral wetting and altered root distribution to drip irrigation on sandy soils.
reference_entries: Zotarelli, L., J.M. Scholberg, M.D. Dukes, R. Muñoz-Carpena, and J. Icerman. 2009. Tomato yield, biomass accumulation, root distribution and water use efficiency on a sandy soil, as affected by nitrogen rate and irrigation scheduling. Agr. Water Mgt. 96:23–34.

links.passage: The use of appropriate irrigation scheduling facilitates more frequent applications of small vol- umes of water and improves matching of water supply and crop water de- mand, which is critical to reduce potential crop water stress and leach- ing losses in sandy soils (Zotarelli et al., 2008a, 2008b, 2009).
supporting_passages: Because applying frequent small-volume irri- gation with conventional systems tends to be labor-intensive and/or technically difficult to use, sensor- based irrigation systems may facilitate the successful use of low-volume, high-frequency irrigation systems in commercial vegetable systems.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence states that frequent small irrigations reduce crop water stress, and the next sentence says sensor-based systems are what make such low-volume high-frequency irrigation feasible.

links.passage: Smajstrla and Locascio (1996) used switching ten- siometers to control drip irrigation of fresh market tomato.
supporting_passages: The highest yields in a 4-year study were achieved with a 1.45 psi tensiometer set point, which is equivalent to 10% volumetric water content for the Arredondo fine sand (hyperthermic Grossarenic Paleudults) at the study site.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence names tensiometer control and the later sentence in the same paragraph reports the highest tomato yields obtained at a given tensiometer set point.

links.passage: When used for vegetable irrigation control on gravelly loam soil in south- ern Florida, granular matrix sensors performed erratically and did not re- duce water application compared with a time-based schedule (Muñoz- Carpena et al., 2005b).

links.passage: Cardenas-Lailhacar et al. (2008) found that granular matrix sensor- based irrigation controllers were no more effective than a rain sensor for turfgrass irrigation control on a fine sand soil.

links.passage: Dukes and Scholberg (2005) installed an automatic irrigation con- trol system based on research grade TDR soil moisture probes and micro- controllers for irrigation of sweet corn.
supporting_passages: This control system was coupled with a subsurface drip irrigation sys- tem with a drip tube buried under each row at 23 and 33 cm in two different treatments.
The 23-cm deep treatment under automatic control reduced irrigation 11% relative to sprinkler irrigation typically used by growers.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence names TDR soil moisture probe control and the later sentences of the same paragraph report the 11% irrigation reduction obtained under that automatic control.
reference_entries: Dukes, M.D. and J.M. Scholberg. 2005. Soil moisture controlled subsurface drip irrigation on sandy soils. Appl. Eng. Agr. 21:89–101.

links.passage: Dukes et al. (2003) used a simple soil moisture-based control system to automatically maintain a rel- atively constant soil moisture content in the root zone of green bell pepper through high-frequency irrigation based on soil moisture measurements by the control system.
supporting_passages: Compared with manual irrigation treatments with one or two irrigation events per day with similar yield, irrigation amount was reduced by 50%.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence names soil moisture-based control and the following sentence reports the 50% reduction in irrigation amount with similar yield.
reference_entries: Dukes, M.D., E.H. Simonne, W.E. Davis, D.W. Studstill, and R. Hochmuth. 2003. Effect of sensor-based high frequency irrigation on bell pepper yield and water use. Proc. Intl. Conf. Irr. Drainage 2:665–674.

links.passage: Similar results reduc- ing irrigation application and drain- age while maintaining green bell pepper yields on sandy soils have been reported for Florida conditions (Dukes et al., 2006).

In general, this study found that a simple and inexpensive irrigation controller coupled with commercially available soil moisture probes (Muñoz- Carpena et al., 2008) was effective at reducing both irrigation water appli- cation and nitrogen leaching under several drip irrigation configurations.

supporting_passages: This results in higher fertilizer use efficiency by the crop as well as a reduction of nutrient leaching be- low the plant root zone.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence describes fertigation through microirrigation and the following sentence states its effect of reducing nutrient leaching below the root zone.
